query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated method that combines high-resolution, modulated differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) with simultaneous high‐temperature dilatometry and calibrated CALPHAD modeling can determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume changes at melting, and key liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys with an uncertainty below 10%, significantly outperforming traditional standalone techniques.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy samples (e.g., equiatomic Cantor alloy) in their well-mixed solid state.
generation.intervention: Subject the samples to modulated DSC and concurrent dilatometric analysis under an inert atmosphere while using CALPHAD modeling to benchmark and fit the experimentally obtained thermal signals.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed over a broad temperature range—from room temperature to above the melting point—using rapid scanning rates and controlled, oxidation-free (inert atmosphere) conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The intrinsically high configurational entropy and atomic-scale disorder inherent to HEAs, which govern their phase stability and melting behavior.
generation.mechanism: Modulated DSC detects detailed heat flow patterns during fusion, and dilatometry records the associated volume changes; integrating these measurements with CALPHAD allows one to account for both thermal and configurational contributions, thereby extracting precise values for melting parameters and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion parameters (melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change) extracted via the integrated method will consistently fall within a ±10% error margin of CALPHAD-based predictions and reference literature values, and will display systematic compositional dependence in line with configurational entropy effects.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC and dilatometry without CALPHAD integration, which typically exhibit uncertainties greater than 20% and are less efficient in capturing complex entropic contributions.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be most effective for single-phase, well-characterized HEAs; its accuracy may decrease in multi-phase or strongly segregating alloys where overlapping transitions obscure the fusion signals.
generation.uncertainty: Calibration challenges and potential impacts of short-range ordering on the DSC signal could introduce uncertainties; further studies will be necessary to generalize the method across all HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of HEA samples (including both equiatomic and non-equiatomic variants) and measure their fusion properties using the integrated modulated DSC/dilatometry method. Independently determine the same fusion parameters using conventional DSC protocols without CALPHAD assistance. Compare both sets of results against CALPHAD predictions and published reference data.
measurements: Heat flow curves from modulated DSC
Volume change profiles from high-temperature dilatometry
Reference fusion property data from literature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated method does not consistently yield fusion parameters (melting point, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change) within ±10% of the CALPHAD predictions and reference values, or if its uncertainty remains comparable to or higher than that of traditional methods, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Senkov et al. demonstrated [] that for high entropy alloys, Calphad computations of type and number of phases agreed well with experimental results only when more than half of binary systems were fully assessed; however, even when there are enough data on binary and ternary systems, Calphad predictions of transformation temperatures, phase compositions and fractions are challenging. Compared with metals, the databases for oxides are much more limited, especially for the temperature range addressed in this study.
